subject: dplyr:summarise behavior differs when operating on data frame vs. data table

messages.author: 6ed2ff7838c0c40e
messages.subject: dplyr:summarise behavior differs when operating on data frame vs. data table
parts:
I'm summarising a data frame with millions of rows. plyr turned out to be too slow, so I tried dplyr, but found differing behavior of the summarise function, depending on whether it operates on a data frame or a data table. Specifically, summarise doesn't correctly count the number of rows by group when fed a data table. I was able to reproduce the behavior with the built-in mtcars dataset, so here's an example:

library(dplyr) 

CASE 1: summarise with a data frame
> summarise(group_by(tbl_df(mtcars), cyl), length(cyl))
# Output follows:
Source: local data frame [3 x 2]

  cyl length(cyl)
1   4          11
2   6           7
3   8          14

CASE 2: summarise with a data table
> summarise(group_by(tbl_dt(mtcars), cyl), length(cyl))
# Output follows:
Source:     local data table [3 x 2]

  cyl length(cyl)
1   4           1
2   6           1
3   8           1

Note that the number of rows for each level of cyl is counted correctly in CASE 1, using a data frame, but not in CASE 2, using a data table. 

I can certainly work with a data frame instead of a data table, but I'd like to know why this is happening. I'm new to dplyr and data table objects. Am I doing something wrong or is this a bug?

Here's my sessionInfo() in case it might be helpful.

> sessionInfo()

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: dplyr:summarise behavior differs when operating on data frame vs. data table
parts:
Hi Joel,

That's because of a different in the way data.tables and data.frames
work - to mask over the difference you can use the new n() function:

summarise(group_by(tbl_df(mtcars), cyl), n())
summarise(group_by(tbl_df(mtcars), cyl), n())

In general, please do report any infelicities since dplyr is still
under active development and the test suite is still growing.

Hadley

Thanks Hadley.

Here are the timings for one of my actual data frames. Timings were done on a 2013 Macbook Pro 15" Retina Display; Core i7, 2.8 GHz; 16 GB 1600 MHz DDR3 RAM; OS X 10.8.5.

Session Info (replace plyr_1.8 with dplyr_0.01, for the dplyr timings):

> sessionInfo()
R version 3.0.1 (2013-05-16)
Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin10.8.0 (64-bit)

locale:
[1] en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/C/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8

attached base packages:
[1] stats graphics grDevices utils datasets methods base

other attached packages:

loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
[1] assertthat_0.1 tools_3.0.1

The data frame has 1.64 million rows and 2 columns. The output object has 1.08 million rows and 3 columns.

> system.time(summarise(group_by(tbl_df(dat_df), emplid, program.action.desc), count=n()))
user system elapsed
15.577 0.284 15.859
> system.time(summarise(group_by(tbl_dt(dat_df), emplid, program.action.desc), count=n()))
user system elapsed
0.979 0.097 1.074
> system.time(ddply(dat_df, .(emplid, program.action.desc), summarise, count=length(emplid)))
Timing stopped at: 440.643 113.409 559.405

Because ddply took so long, I reran the timings with a subset of the data with about 139,000 rows. Here are those timings:

> system.time(summarise(group_by(tbl_df(dat_df), emplid, program.action.desc), count=n()))
user system elapsed
0.660 0.023 0.684
> system.time(summarise(group_by(tbl_dt(dat_df), emplid, program.action.desc), count=n()))
user system elapsed
0.056 0.006 0.062
> system.time(ddply(dat_df, .(emplid, program.action.desc), summarise, count=length(emplid)))
user system elapsed
23.197 8.623 31.820

Let me know if I can provide any additional information.

Joel

messages.subject: Re: dplyr:summarise behavior differs when operating on data frame vs. data table
parts:
Thanks - that agrees with my timings on pseudo-realistic examples:
dplyr is 20-100x faster than plyr, and switching to data table gains
about another 10x.

I've been working with Romain Francois to make the data frame
aggregation even faster, and it looks like we might be able to beat
data table by another 2-10x.

Hadley
